card.hook: You can nearly miss the start of the Monkey Forest because the street around it is so busy: cafés, galleries, and one chunky stone sign saying you've arrived. Grab this frame first, because it tells your photo album exactly where you were.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jalan Monkey Forest, near the main entrance at the southern end of the street, and look for the stone entrance sign. Face south-west, because that's where the sanctuary lies.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the sign and the street. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you want the whole entrance and the shopfronts in one go.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the stone sign off-centre, so the street and shopfronts fill the rest of the picture.
card.best_time: The street outside is quieter than the forest itself, so it's a relaxed place to take your time over this shot.
card.selfie_here: Head onto the stone bridge over the ravine and stand near the two stone dragon statues at its front end, with the ravine and jungle behind you. Use your front camera, hold it a little low and switch to its wider setting if it has one, so the dragons and the greenery both fit.
card.rules_and_safety: Never offer food, keep your distance and avoid eye contact, because the macaques may grab bags or climb on visitors. Don't reach out to touch them, as they may scratch or bite. Flash isn't allowed, and the temple areas are for worship only, so shoot the Pura Dalem Agung Padangtegal gateway from just outside.
card.challenge: Get the stone sign off-centre with a café peeking in beside it, then see if you can find a dragon-headed railing inside to match.
card.good_to_know: The Monkey Forest is a village-owned sanctuary of about 10 hectares with at least 115 tree species. As of 2023 about 1,260 macaques lived here. Its three Hindu temples are all thought to date from around 1350.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jalan Monkey Forest, near the main entrance at the southern end of the street, and look for the stone entrance sign. Face south-west, because that's where the sanctuary lies.

selfie_spots.why: Several guides single this concrete-and-stone bridge out as one of the sanctuary's best photo backdrops, and the dragon statues add a distinctive frame.

card.hook: Picture a royal family's home with its front door right on a busy town road, scooters buzzing past carved stone walls and tall gates. That's Ubud Palace, and you can see the whole show from the pavement.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement directly opposite the palace front on Jalan Raya Ubud. Face the carved walls and tall gates so the whole frontage fits in your shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the palace front as you see it. If the pavement is too narrow for the full gates and walls, tap 0.5x, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the carvings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the gate up with the centre of the frame and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is a good bet for softer light and fewer people on the pavement. The main pavilion usually hosts dance shows at night, but photography can be restricted during live performances, so ask first.
card.selfie_here: Try the street side across the road from the Ubud Art Market, facing the split gate (candi bentar) on Jalan Raya Ubud. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the gate over your shoulder. It's a best-fit spot, not an official selfie spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Jalan Raya Ubud by the market, while you stand in front of the split gate on the palace side of the road.
card.rules_and_safety: Take care crossing the road. The palace is opposite the main entrance to Ubud Art Market and traffic is often heavy. One guide says selfie sticks are allowed, but check on arrival. Photography can be restricted in sacred areas and during live performances.
card.challenge: Find the gate's symmetry, then take one wide shot and one close-up of the carved stone. Can you tell which one your friends will like more?
card.good_to_know: Ubud Palace is officially called Puri Saren Agung and was the home of Ubud's royal family. The present palace dates from the reign of Tjokorda Putu Kandel (1800–1823). It was badly damaged in the 1917 earthquake, quickly restored, and opened to foreign guests in 1928. Many of the stone carvings are the work of local artist I Gusti Nyoman Lempad.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement directly opposite the palace front on Jalan Raya Ubud. Face the carved walls and tall gates so the whole frontage fits in your shot.

card.hook: Picture a row of stone women pouring water into a pool, tucked in a green hollow, each one standing for a holy river. It's the kind of tidy, repeating scene your phone loves.
card.stand_here: At Goa Gajah, stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Then walk to the steps just above the bathing pools and face the row of spouts and statues, with the green garden behind them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole row of spouts and statues. If the pools feel too tight to fit, tap 0.5x, and use 2x for details like a single carved figure or the demon face over the cave doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and centre yourself on the middle of the pools, so both rows of spouts sit evenly either side.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is quieter, with fewer big groups at the pools than around midday. Getting there early gives you a cleaner frame.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the bathing pool in the main courtyard with your back to the carved cave entrance, so the demon face looms over your shoulder. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more carving in, and hold the phone a little higher.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friend or a kind passer-by to stand on the stone stairs that step down into the courtyard while you stand by the pool, so the carved cave entrance and the pool both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep the flash off, especially around people praying, and ask before photographing worshippers. Don't block the cave doorway for long poses. Selfie sticks are listed as 'not encouraged' here. Shaded steps can stay damp and slippery, so wear shoes with grip and expect stairs.
card.challenge: Get both rows of spouts perfectly balanced on the gridlines, then check whether you can spot the gap where the lost statue once stood.
card.good_to_know: Goa Gajah, the Elephant Cave, is generally dated to the 9th to 11th centuries and mixes Hindu and Buddhist imagery. The carved face around the cave mouth is thought to ward off evil spirits. Dutch archaeologists rediscovered the cave in 1923, but the bathing pools weren't uncovered until 1954.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: At Goa Gajah, stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Then walk to the steps just above the bathing pools and face the row of spouts and statues, with the green garden behind them.

card.hook: Most people hurry past the temple to get to the famous path, but the carved walls and tiered meru shrines at the start are worth a few photos on their own. Then the ridge opens up into tall grass and valley, and it feels like a different walk.
card.stand_here: Start at the entrance of Pura Gunung Lebah, the temple at the southern start of the walk, and face the carved walls and meru shrines with the start of the ridge path beside them.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x at the temple entrance so the walls and towers fit without you backing into the path. Switch to zoom 1x for the path and palm trees, and try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for carved details or to stack up the layers of the valley.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the temple wall on one third of the frame with the path leading off the other, and tap the carved stonework, then slide it darker if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the path. Guides disagree on the perfect hour, so pick whichever suits you, and stay to daylight hours, which one guide recommends for safety and visibility.
card.selfie_here: Walk about 1 km along the ridge path to the two palm trees, which guides call the trail's most popular photo spot. Use the front camera at 0.5x, and on your return leg face south so the open valley and hills sit behind you.
card.ask_someone: At the south end of the trail, stand by the stairs on the temple's east side and ask a passer-by to take your photo with the ridge path running behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Pura Gunung Lebah is a place of worship, so dress modestly and respect any signs. It may be closed for renovation, so check the official site or local signs before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get both palm trees framed neatly on either side of the paved path, with the path leading your eye straight into the valley?
card.good_to_know: The Campuhan Ridge Walk is a paved path along a ridge in Ubud, between tall grass with the valley beyond. One guide says the temple was under renovation, so you could photograph the outside but not go in, though that may have changed. If you want a wider view of countryside and rice fields, Karsa Kafe at the northern end is another recommended spot, but it's a longer walk.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the entrance of Pura Gunung Lebah, the temple at the southern start of the walk, and face the carved walls and meru shrines with the start of the ridge path beside them. The phone icon on the map is to the north along the ridge path, about 1 km (985 m) on foot.

card.hook: Scooters buzz past, shoppers drift by, and bright goods spill out toward the road. Ubud Market is never still, which is exactly why it's fun to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand at the front of Puri Saren Agung palace on Jalan Raya Ubud and face across the road. The market is across the road to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic frontage shot. Try zoom 2x for close-ups of stalls and goods, and drop to zoom 0.5x in the narrow lane on Jalan Karna, where you can't step back.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest stall, then slide it a touch darker so the colours stay rich, and turn on gridlines to keep the frontage along the lower third.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when local trade is under way before the souvenir stalls open. You'll get a quieter, more everyday scene.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at the market's carved entrance gate (Raya Ubud No.35) with the gate behind you. For a burst of colour, stand at the sarong stall inside with the draped fabrics over your shoulder, and try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from the front of Puri Saren Agung, with you placed so the market is in frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone in a pocket or wrist strap while you walk through the lanes. One older report says selfie sticks are fine at the market, but check on arrival, and check for closures on the day.
card.challenge: Find the most colourful stall and grab three frames: one wide at zoom 1x, one close at zoom 2x, and one with a scooter zipping past.
card.good_to_know: Ubud Market sits on the main road in the centre of Ubud, with stalls and shopfronts packed along the street. At the main corner on Jalan Raya Ubud, newer multi-storey buildings mix with passing street life. Jalan Karna is a narrow lane lined with stalls, so it's great for a close, colourful view.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the front of Puri Saren Agung palace on Jalan Raya Ubud and face across the road. The market is across the road to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot.

selfie_spots.why: The carved gate gives a distinctive backdrop with the market's entrance behind you.

card.hook: Picture a pond full of lotus leaves, three red-brick gateways rising behind it, and a café terrace where you can sit with a drink and take it all in. That's the Ubud Water Palace, and the terrace is the calm way to see it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Café Lotus terrace, on the western side of the lotus pond, and face across the water toward the temple. You're looking slightly down at it, which gives a wider, calmer view than the walkway. It's a paid spot, so plan to buy something while you're there.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the pond, gateways and roofs in one go. Try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the gates and carvings. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want lots of foreground water or leaves.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the water in the lower third and the gateways along the upper line, and keep the roof lines level.
card.best_time: Sunset or golden hour is the time to aim for. The lotus flowers are said to bloom roughly June to September, and outside those months the pond can look bare, so let the temple be the star.
card.selfie_here: Walk to about halfway down the central stone walkway through the lotus pond. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the temple gate over your shoulder for a nice symmetrical shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the raised platform on the bridge just outside the temple gate, before you go in, so they can fit the pond, walkway and temple into one photo.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine at the lotus pond and at Kori Agung, but not in the area reserved for prayer, and don't climb onto any altar or shrine. Stay on the walkway rather than stepping onto the pond edges, and don't take photos or videos inside the temple without permission. The grounds are ticketed, so check the official site for current prices, opening hours and dress rules.
card.challenge: Build a three-layer shot: frangipani flowers or leaves up front, the pond in the middle, and the gateways behind.
card.good_to_know: Pura Taman Saraswati is a Balinese Hindu temple dedicated to Sarasvati, the goddess of learning, literature and art. It was designed by the Balinese sculptor and architect I Gusti Nyoman Lempad and built between 1951 and 1952. Look for the three red-brick gateways, with the tallest in the middle between two frangipani trees.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Café Lotus terrace, on the western side of the lotus pond, and face across the water toward the temple. You're looking slightly down at it, which gives a wider, calmer view than the walkway. It's a paid spot, so plan to buy something while you're there.

card.hook: Stand in the middle of Puri Lukisan and slowly turn on the spot. There's a building on every side, like a very civilised art carousel.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the Puri Lukisan Museum site. Turn slowly and you'll see the buildings to the north, west, east and south in turn.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x to fit a whole building in, then 1x for doorways. Go to 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the murals and carved figures.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines to keep the building edges straight, and if bright sky is washing out the walls, tap the wall and slide it a touch darker.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. Midday sun can leave deep shadows around doorways and roofs, so nudge the brightness if that happens.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of the lotus pond in front of the West Hall, with the hall behind you. For another backdrop, try the small pond in the central courtyard, with its traditional statue and the museum buildings behind you. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the landmark over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back across the courtyard while you stand at the edge of the courtyard lotus pond, so the four museum buildings fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash inside the museum. Photo rules inside the galleries can differ from the grounds, so check the official site before you go and follow any signs once you're in.
card.challenge: Spin on the spot and take one photo of each building: north, west, east and south. That's four shots, four galleries and no walking.
card.good_to_know: Puri Lukisan shows traditional and modern Balinese painting and wood carving, with works from the 1930s onwards. The architect and artist I Gusti Nyoman Lempad designed parts of the museum and painted the murals at the entrance to the North Building. The four buildings are the Pitamaha Gallery, the Ida Bagus Made Gallery, the Wayang Gallery and the Founders Gallery.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the Puri Lukisan Museum site. Turn slowly and you'll see the buildings to the north, west, east and south in turn.

selfie_spots.why: A visitor describes this pond as a sight to behold, and the West Hall is the museum's most photogenic building in their account.

selfie_research.notes: The sources do not name a selfie stick rule, so none is given. The pages describe the pond and courtyard as photogenic but do not say where a selfie should be framed, so the 'landmark behind you' positions are my inference from their descriptions. card.hook: Picture this: you're in a garden in Ubud, a parrot hops onto your shoulder, and a museum full of paintings is waiting just behind you. Not a bad start for a photo stop.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Blanco Renaissance Museum, because the phone icon on the map is the museum itself (about 0 minutes on foot once you arrive). Face the building and take a step back if you can, so it doesn't get cut off at the edges.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the building as you see it. If you're too close to fit it all in, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details that catch your eye.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright, so the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon is usually kinder than midday, when the light is harsh and the shadows are strong.
card.selfie_here: Head for the garden with the parrots, just before the main gallery building. Use the front camera and let a parrot perch on your shoulder; guides say the staff will help with the shot. For a second pose, stand on the terrace beside the gilded Balinese dancer statues with the building behind you, and try 0.5x so more of it fits in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the entry path and frame the whole entrance, while you stand at the gate by the stone dragons.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are not allowed inside the main gallery, and flash is prohibited there, but the gardens and outdoor areas are fine. Some private residence sections of the house don't allow photos at all, so keep to any signs and check with staff on arrival.
card.challenge: Find one colour or pattern that feels like it belongs in a painting and fill the whole frame with it. Bonus points if a parrot photobombs.
card.good_to_know: The Blanco Renaissance Museum is an art museum in Ubud, Bali, devoted to the painter Antonio Blanco. It opened on 28 December 1998. You may also hear it called the Don Antonio Blanco Museum, which is handy if you're asking for directions.
